members.description:
The consumer's callback, invoked after the state is applied.

Not an attribute: it is a function. And not reachable from React's JSX,
which reserves every `on[A-Z]` prop for its own event system and drops
what it does not recognise; the generated wrapper listens for the events
instead.

members.name: requestOpen
members.description:

Announces before it acts, so `preventDefault()` on the `helix-open` or

element then updates itself; in controlled mode it applies nothing and
waits for the consumer to pass a new `open`, which is what "controlled"
means.

members.name: chevronPlacement
members.description:

`auto` resolves to `end`, which is where a reader scanning a list of
summaries expects it: the label starts at the same x on every row, and the
indicator is found once at the edge rather than shifting with the text.

`none` is for a row that carries its own affordance and would otherwise
have two.

members.name: renderChevron

members.name: accordion
members.description:
The nearest accordion above this item, if there is one.

Resolved on demand rather than held, so an item moved between accordions
coordinates with the one it is in now. `closest` crosses no shadow
boundary, which is correct: an item inside another item's content is in
that item's light DOM and finds the same accordion, so the check below is
what keeps it independent.

members.name: peers
members.description:
The items this one coordinates with: its own siblings, and only those.

Direct children only. An accordion nested inside an item's content is a
separate set, and opening a section in it must not close anything outside.

members.name: handleToggle
members.description:
Opens or closes this item, and enforces the accordion's mode.

The item that was clicked is the coordinator. It refuses first, then
announces, then applies, then closes its peers, in that order: closing a
peer before knowing whether this change was even allowed would leave the
set collapsed after a listener refused it.

members.name: focusTrigger
members.description:

The parent accordion drives arrow-key navigation and cannot reach the
trigger itself, because it is inside this item's shadow root. Exposing the
intent as a method keeps the parent out of the child's internals.

members.name: internals
members.description:
The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,
so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

members.name: touched
members.description:
Whether the reader has had a go at the field yet.

This was `:user-invalid`, which is the platform's own answer to "is this
field wrong *yet*" and is the right idea. It does not work here, and the
reason is structural rather than a browser bug: `:user-invalid` tracks
interaction with the element it is on, and nobody interacts with this
element. The reader types into an `<input>` inside its shadow root, so
the host's interaction flag is never set and the selector never matches.
Measured after submitting an invalid required field and again after
editing one and leaving it: false both times, while `:invalid` matched
both times.

So the moments are listened for instead, and both of them demonstrably
reach the host: `invalid` when a form is submitted with this control
failing, and `change` when the reader has edited and committed. Focus
alone is deliberately not one of them. Tabbing past an empty required
field should not be answered with an error.

Reading the static the platform itself reads to decide, rather than
probing: `validity` and `validationMessage` throw `NotSupportedError` on
an element that is not form-associated, and a group whose members each
submit themselves is not. Such a control still shows a message, it just
has to be given one.

reads as a description it cannot find.

members.name: renderGroupLabel
members.description:
A label over a set rather than beside a control.

A plain element and not a `<label for>`, because a group is not a single
control and there is nothing for `for` to point at. What names the group
is `linkHost`, pointing the host's internals at this element.

members.name: renderLabel
members.description:
A label above the control, pointing at it.

A real `<label for>`, so pressing the words focuses the field and the
browser does the forwarding. It resolves because `for` looks within the
same tree, and the control it names is in this shadow root.

**Nothing at all when there is no label**, which is the same rule the
hint and the feedback follow: none of the three is always used, and an
element rendered empty is not free. It still generates a box, so it still
takes a row of the grid and a gap on either side of it, which is a field
that has moved down the page for a label nobody wrote. `nothing` leaves
comment markers rather than a node, so the gap has nothing to sit between.

Naming a control without showing the label is `hide-label`, not an empty
one: an unnamed field is a field a screen reader announces as "edit text".

members.name: renderHint
members.description:
Help under the control, unless something has gone wrong.

The two share a place rather than stacking, so a field is one line of
small text either way and nothing below it moves when the message
changes. What the reader needs at that moment is what is wrong, and a
hint that survives the error it describes is a second line to read before
getting to the one that matters.

members.name: renderFeedback
members.description:
The validation message, in the hint's place.

`role="alert"` rather than a live region on the whole field, so what is
announced is the message and not the label and help along with it.

members.name: linkHost
members.description:
Points the host at its own label and description nodes, for a group.

A control's `<input>` and its hint are both in the shadow root, so a
plain `aria-describedby` resolves between them. A group's host is in the
light DOM and its hint is not, so the IDREF cannot reach and
`element.ariaDescribedByElements` drops the reference outright. Only the
`ElementInternals` form keeps it, measured in Chrome 148: two of two
kept through internals, zero of one through the element.

Client only, and deliberately, because element references need the nodes
to exist and on the server they do not. The name is therefore also set as
a plain string by the component, which a server can write, and the
reference here overrides it wherever a consumer slotted something richer
than a string. A group with only a property for a label reads the same
either way.

members.name: refreshFeedback
members.description:

Validity changes through `ElementInternals` rather than through a
property, so nothing schedules an update for it. Worse, the order is
against us: this mixin sits above the control in the prototype chain, so
its `updated` runs before the control's own, which is where `setValidity`
is called. Reading the verdict here would always read the previous one,
which is what left a corrected field still showing the error it had
before. So the control says when it has reported, and this schedules the
one further update that needs. It converges because the second pass finds
nothing changed.

have to be reconciled rather than simply written over.

members.name: applyTemplate
members.description:
Writes the track list into the shadow root's own stylesheet.

Into a `<style>` rather than onto `this.style`, and the difference is
hydration. An inline style on the host is an attribute the element gives
itself once it upgrades, so a React consumer's server markup does not have
it and hydration reports a mismatch it will not patch up. The shadow root
is not part of the tree React hydrates, so a rule written there is free.

The element is filled imperatively because Lit refuses expressions inside
`<style>`: it is an invalid binding location and throws while rendering
rather than at build time. Hence a static, empty element in the template
and its `textContent` set here.

It sets a custom property rather than the track list itself. A shadow
root's adopted stylesheets cascade *after* its own `<style>` elements, and
`static styles` is adopted, so a `grid-template-columns` here lost to the
one in the stylesheet and every `min` grid came out a single column. The
stylesheet only ever reads `--_grid-template`, so there is nothing to
lose against.

The consequence is that a server-rendered grid falls back to the
stylesheet's single column until it upgrades. That is why `columns` is also
expressed as plain CSS below: the fixed-count case, which can be enumerated,
needs no JavaScript at all, and only `min` depends on this.

members.name: touched
members.description:
Whether the reader has had a go at the field yet.

This was `:user-invalid`, which is the platform's own answer to "is this
field wrong *yet*" and is the right idea. It does not work here, and the
reason is structural rather than a browser bug: `:user-invalid` tracks
interaction with the element it is on, and nobody interacts with this
element. The reader types into an `<input>` inside its shadow root, so
the host's interaction flag is never set and the selector never matches.
Measured after submitting an invalid required field and again after
editing one and leaving it: false both times, while `:invalid` matched
both times.

So the moments are listened for instead, and both of them demonstrably
reach the host: `invalid` when a form is submitted with this control
failing, and `change` when the reader has edited and committed. Focus
alone is deliberately not one of them. Tabbing past an empty required
field should not be answered with an error.

members.name: validates
members.description:
Whether this element may be asked about its own validity at all.

Reading the static the platform itself reads to decide, rather than
probing: `validity` and `validationMessage` throw `NotSupportedError` on
an element that is not form-associated, and a group whose members each
submit themselves is not. Such a control still shows a message, it just
has to be given one.

members.name: resolvedFeedback
members.description: The message actually shown: the consumer's, or the platform's, or none.

members.name: describedBy
members.description:
Id of the description node, for `aria-describedby` on the control.

One at a time, because only one of the two is ever rendered. Naming both
would point a screen reader at an id that resolves to nothing, which it
reads as a description it cannot find.

members.name: renderGroupLabel
members.description:
A label over a set rather than beside a control.

A plain element and not a `<label for>`, because a group is not a single
control and there is nothing for `for` to point at. What names the group
is `linkHost`, pointing the host's internals at this element.

members.name: renderLabel
members.description:
A label above the control, pointing at it.

A real `<label for>`, so pressing the words focuses the field and the
browser does the forwarding. It resolves because `for` looks within the
same tree, and the control it names is in this shadow root.

**Nothing at all when there is no label**, which is the same rule the
hint and the feedback follow: none of the three is always used, and an
element rendered empty is not free. It still generates a box, so it still
takes a row of the grid and a gap on either side of it, which is a field
that has moved down the page for a label nobody wrote. `nothing` leaves
comment markers rather than a node, so the gap has nothing to sit between.

Naming a control without showing the label is `hide-label`, not an empty
one: an unnamed field is a field a screen reader announces as "edit text".

members.name: renderHint
members.description:
Help under the control, unless something has gone wrong.

The two share a place rather than stacking, so a field is one line of
small text either way and nothing below it moves when the message
changes. What the reader needs at that moment is what is wrong, and a
hint that survives the error it describes is a second line to read before
getting to the one that matters.

members.name: renderFeedback
members.description:
The validation message, in the hint's place.

`role="alert"` rather than a live region on the whole field, so what is
announced is the message and not the label and help along with it.

members.name: linkHost
members.description:
Points the host at its own label and description nodes, for a group.

A control's `<input>` and its hint are both in the shadow root, so a
plain `aria-describedby` resolves between them. A group's host is in the
light DOM and its hint is not, so the IDREF cannot reach and
`element.ariaDescribedByElements` drops the reference outright. Only the
`ElementInternals` form keeps it, measured in Chrome 148: two of two
kept through internals, zero of one through the element.

Client only, and deliberately, because element references need the nodes
to exist and on the server they do not. The name is therefore also set as
a plain string by the component, which a server can write, and the
reference here overrides it wherever a consumer slotted something richer
than a string. A group with only a property for a label reads the same
either way.

members.name: shownFeedback
members.description: What the last render put on screen, so a change can be noticed.

members.name: refreshFeedback
members.description:
Re-reads the platform's verdict, for a control that has just reported one.

Validity changes through `ElementInternals` rather than through a
property, so nothing schedules an update for it. Worse, the order is
against us: this mixin sits above the control in the prototype chain, so
its `updated` runs before the control's own, which is where `setValidity`
is called. Reading the verdict here would always read the previous one,
which is what left a corrected field still showing the error it had
before. So the control says when it has reported, and this schedules the
one further update that needs. It converges because the second pass finds
nothing changed.

members.description:

members.name: renderLabel
members.description:

members.name: linkHost

a plain string by the component, which a server can write, and the
reference here overrides it wherever a consumer slotted something richer
than a string. A group with only a property for a label reads the same
either way.

members.name: shownFeedback

members.name: refreshFeedback
members.description:

property, so nothing schedules an update for it. Worse, the order is
against us: this mixin sits above the control in the prototype chain, so

which is what left a corrected field still showing the error it had
before. So the control says when it has reported, and this schedules the

nothing changed.

declarations.description:
Two properties, and they answer different questions. `as` is the element, which decides the document outline and what a screen reader announces. `appearance` is the treatment, which decides size, weight, leading, and tracking together. They are separate because they genuinely come apart: a section's second heading sometimes has to look smaller without lying about the outline, and a `

` sometimes has to read as a caption. They default to matching, so the common case is `as="h2"` and nothing else. The pairing is resolved in CSS rather than by computing an attribute, so the element writes nothing to its own host: `as="h2"` picks up the heading ramp through a selector, and setting `appearance` takes the pairing rule out of play. Deriving it in `willUpdate` worked, but it put an attribute on the host that the server's markup did not have, which is a hydration mismatch in every React consumer. **Size, weight, and leading are not properties.** Exposing them separately offers a few hundred combinations of which a handful are right, and every caller then picks one. An appearance is a decision the system already made: the ramp is named, and a page built from it is consistent because there was nothing else to choose. `tone` stays separate, because color carries state rather than typography. Folding it in would mean `caption-danger` and `label-primary` and the rest of the cross product, which is the explosion `appearance` exists to prevent.

members.description:
Whether the reader has had a go at the field yet.

field wrong *yet*" and is the right idea. It does not work here, and the
reason is structural rather than a browser bug: `:user-invalid` tracks
interaction with the element it is on, and nobody interacts with this
element. The reader types into an `<input>` inside its shadow root, so
the host's interaction flag is never set and the selector never matches.

editing one and leaving it: false both times, while `:invalid` matched
both times.

reach the host: `invalid` when a form is submitted with this control
failing, and `change` when the reader has edited and committed. Focus
alone is deliberately not one of them. Tabbing past an empty required
field should not be answered with an error.

no property here, so nothing would schedule the update that re-reads it. A
consumer rendering the bubble's content after this upgrades, which is what
a framework does, would leave the trigger describing nothing.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

members.name: requestActive
members.description:
Requests a new current item, and reports whether the request stood.

Announces before it acts, so `preventDefault()` on the `helix-change` is
a refusal and nothing moves. Unlike a native control, nothing has moved
by the time this runs, so refusing is simply not writing: there is
nothing to put back.

members.name: resolveActive
members.description:
Which item is current, given what there is to choose from.

The first enabled one when `value` names nothing, which is a set before
its consumer has chosen and a set whose current item has just been
removed. Disabled items are skipped in the fallback but not in the match:
a consumer who names a disabled item meant it, and quietly moving to
another would be the component overruling them.

members.name: chevron
members.description:
Which end of a row the chevron sits at.

Unset is the start, which is what a tree of folders looks like. `end` puts
it at the far side, where it reads as a control belonging to the row rather
than as part of the name, and it lets every label start at one place
without a row that has no chevron reserving space for one.

On the tree rather than on each item, because a row whose chevron sat
somewhere different from its siblings' would be a mistake, not a choice.

members.name: syncItems
members.description:
Pushes tree-owned state down: which item is selected, which holds the tab
stop, and how deep each one sits.

Depth is computed here rather than by each item counting its own ancestors,
so an item moved in the tree gets the right indent without knowing it moved.
